title: BGP/MPLS IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)
summary: Describes how a service provider can use an IP backbone to offer IP virtual private networks. It uses a peer model: customer edge routers send routes to provider edge routers, no overlay is visible to the customer's routing, and sites do not peer with each other. It obsoletes RFC 2547 and is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone company runs one big network but gives each business the feel of its own private one. Each business's traffic stays separate from the others.

questions: what is a route target in mpls vpn
subtitle: How a provider runs many customers' private IP networks over one shared MPLS backbone, using BGP to carry the routes.

tldr.problem: A service provider wants to offer customers private IP networks over a shared backbone, even when customers reuse the same addresses, without making each customer manage tunnels between sites.
tldr.mechanism: Customer edge routers give their routes to provider edge routers. The PEs keep a separate table (VRF) per VPN, prefix each route with an 8-byte Route Distinguisher, share them with BGP, and forward traffic inside MPLS label stacks so core routers need no VPN routes.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2547 and is updated by RFC 4577, RFC 4684 and RFC 5462. The design lets no single router hold all VPN routes, so the VPN count is not limited by one device.

today: RFC 4364 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2547. It has been updated by RFC 4577, RFC 4684 and RFC 5462, and no later RFC replaces it.

sections.title: The Peer Model for IP VPNs
sections.content:
RFC 4364 describes how a Service Provider (SP) can use an IP backbone to provide IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs). It uses a peer model: the customers' edge routers (CE routers) send their routes to the provider's edge routers (PE routers). The SP uses BGP to exchange the routes of a particular VPN among the PEs attached to it, in a way that keeps routes from different VPNs distinct even if their address spaces overlap.

CE routers do not peer with each other, so a VPN is not an overlay on the SP's network and the customer has no virtual backbone to manage. Routers inside the backbone that do not attach to CEs are P routers. Each VPN route is assigned an MPLS label, and packets are tunneled across the backbone, so P routers do not need to know the VPN routes.

The scope is a customer who explicitly buys VPN service, and the backbone provides an IP service rather than a layer 2 service. A site may be in more than one VPN, such as an intranet plus several extranets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each office plugs into the phone company's edge box. The boxes in the middle just pass sealed parcels along without knowing which business sent them.

sections.title: VRFs: One Forwarding Table per VPN
sections.content:
Each PE router keeps several forwarding tables: one default forwarding table and a number of VPN Routing and Forwarding tables (VRFs). Every PE/CE attachment circuit is associated, by configuration, with one or more VRFs. In the typical case it is exactly one. A packet arriving on that circuit has its destination looked up in the associated VRF, called its ingress VRF.

A packet arriving on a circuit with no VRF is looked up in the default table, which one can think of as holding the public routes. Connectivity is limited by controlling which routes go into each VRF. A VRF should hold only routes to sites that share at least one VPN with the site it serves.

The PE must decide the attachment circuit from the physical interface and, possibly, parts of the layer 2 header such as a Frame Relay DLCI. The customer must not be able to fool the SP by writing header fields, so those values are set to ones the SP specifies. A customer site can also be split into "virtual sites" that use, for example, different VLANs to select different VRFs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each business gets its own notebook at the edge box, listing only the places that business may reach. The box looks in the right notebook for each parcel.

sections.title: Route Distinguishers and VPN-IPv4 Addresses
sections.content:
Two VPNs may use the same IPv4 prefix for different systems, and BGP must not treat those routes as comparable. The RFC introduces the VPN-IPv4 address family. A VPN-IPv4 address is 12 bytes: an 8-byte Route Distinguisher (RD) followed by a 4-byte IPv4 address. Because VPN-IPv4 and IPv4 are different address families, BGP never compares them.

An RD is only a number. It does not say where a route came from or who may receive it. It lets BGP carry several routes to the same IPv4 prefix, one per VPN, and can also give one system two different routes, for example one for intranet traffic and one for extranet traffic. An RD has a 2-byte type field and a 6-byte value field. Types 0, 1 and 2 are defined: type 0 pairs a 2-byte Autonomous System number with a 4-byte assigned number, type 1 pairs a 4-byte IP address with a 2-byte assigned number, and type 2 pairs a 4-byte AS number with a 2-byte assigned number. BGP ignores this structure when it compares prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: Two companies might both have a room called 'Room 5'. Putting each company's name tag in front keeps the mail from getting mixed up.

sections.title: Distributing Routes with BGP and Route Targets
sections.content:
A PE learns a VPN's routes from the attached CE, converts them to VPN-IPv4 routes and exports them into BGP. At other PEs, the chosen routes are converted back and imported into VRFs. Which VRFs get a route is decided by Route Targets (RTs), BGP Extended Community attributes. A route may carry several RTs but only one RD. Each VRF has a set of export targets attached to routes it originates and a set of import targets that decides which received routes it accepts. The two sets are distinct and need not be the same.

Choosing the targets shapes the VPN. For a fully meshed closed user group, one RT is both import and export on every VRF. For hub and spoke, the hub's VRFs export "Hub" and import "Spoke", and the spokes do the opposite.

PEs exchange the routes over IBGP, either fully meshed or through route reflectors. A PE uses its own address as the BGP next hop and distributes an MPLS label with each route, so it advertises labeled VPN-IPv4 routes. They are carried in BGP Multiprotocol Extensions with AFI 1 and SAFI 128. A PE should not install a VPN-IPv4 route unless one of its VRFs has a matching import target, so no PE needs every route for every VPN. Adding or removing an import target (VPN Join or Prune) is non-disruptive when route refresh is used. Route reflectors can be partitioned by Route Target, so none needs all routes either.
sections.plainLanguage: Each parcel gets colored stickers. A box only keeps parcels whose sticker color it has asked for, so every box only deals with its own business's mail.

sections.title: Forwarding Across the Backbone
sections.content:
When a PE receives an IP packet from a CE, it looks the destination up in the VRF for that attachment circuit. If the next hop is on the same PE, the packet is sent out the egress circuit with no labels. Otherwise the route has a BGP next hop that assigned a "VPN route label", and the packet becomes an MPLS packet carrying that label.

The packet must then be tunneled to the BGP next hop. With an MPLS backbone, PEs advertise /32 prefixes for themselves in the IGP, and a "tunnel label" is pushed on top, unless the BGP next hop is also the IGP next hop and penultimate hop popping is used. Implementations MUST support LDP for setting up the label switched paths. Without MPLS in the core, the packet can be tunneled using MPLS in IP or GRE. At the egress PE, the VPN route label tells which attachment circuit, or which VRF to look in, and the packet leaves as plain IP again.

Because VPN-labeled packets are tunneled, P routers hold only routes to PEs and need none for the VPNs. The specification does not require point-to-point tunnels, explicit tunnel setup or tunnel-specific signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: The edge box puts the parcel in an envelope marked with the delivery address, then in a second envelope for the road. Middle boxes read only the outer envelope.

sections.title: Learning Routes from CEs and Reaching the Internet
sections.content:
A PE can learn a site's routes by static configuration, RIP, OSPF or BGP. BGP between PE and CE works for stub VPNs and transit VPNs, and has several advantages, such as not needing a PE routing instance per CE. Routes from a VPN are not leaked into the backbone's IGP. A Site of Origin attribute can mark routes by site, so a route is never sent back to the site it came from.

Section 9 covers carriers' carriers, where a VPN is itself an ISP or VPN provider and its CE routers must support MPLS. Section 10 covers VPNs that span several Autonomous Systems with three options of increasing scalability: VRF-to-VRF connections between ASBRs, EBGP redistribution of labeled VPN-IPv4 routes, and multi-hop EBGP between PEs.

Section 11 describes four ways a VPN site can reach the public Internet. Section 12 describes a management VPN. By default, no routes are exchanged between a VRF and the default forwarding table.
sections.plainLanguage: A customer can tell the edge box where its rooms are in several ways. There are also special setups for big customers who are phone companies themselves and for reaching the public street.

sections.title: Isolation and Security
sections.content:
The goal is security equal to a layer 2 backbone such as Frame Relay: absent misconfiguration or deliberate interconnection, systems in one VPN cannot reach systems in another. This depends on three conditions. First, a backbone router does not accept labeled packets from a link unless that link attaches only to trusted systems or the packet will leave the backbone before lower labels or the IP header are inspected. Second, labeled VPN-IPv4 routes are not accepted from untrusted peers. Third, the control plane has not been successfully attacked.

The architecture does not encrypt data or detect tampering. Cryptography can be applied CE to CE, and PE to PE is left for further study. If MPLS-in-IP or GRE tunnels are used, an implementation MUST include IPsec, or else MUST let the egress PE validate the source address of tunneled packets. For the control plane, BGP and LDP should not be run with untrusted peers, and the TCP MD5 option should be used with both.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping mail separate does not hide what is inside the envelope. If you also need secrecy, you have to lock the contents yourself.
